clue.text: Drunk given clothing, one trying not to disturb the bar?

definitions.text: one trying not to disturb the bar

blocks.note: high can mean intoxicated
a jumper is a knitted sweater, an item of clothing

explanation.surface: A drunk is handed some clothes, and the question is whether they will make trouble at the pub counter.
explanation.walkthrough: The bar looks like a pub counter, but it is the crossbar in athletics that this athlete tries not to knock off.
explanation.definitionFit: An athlete in this field event clears a raised crossbar and fails if it is dislodged.

clue.text: Loves holding unaccompanied note in romantic song

indicators.note: something holding other things keeps them inside it, so the loves wrap round what follows

blocks.note: love is zero in tennis, written O; two of them here
sole means alone
the third note of the sol-fa scale

explanation.surface: A lover's serenade holds a long solo note.
explanation.walkthrough: The first O and the last O surround SOLE and MI together, giving O SOLE MIO.
explanation.definitionFit: O Sole Mio is a famous Neapolitan ballad, often sung as a passionate love serenade.

clue.text: Try stuffing pastry in container for liquid

indicators.note: stuffing goes inside something, so the attempt is put inside the pastry

blocks.note: a flan is an open pastry tart
to have a go is to try

explanation.surface: Someone attempts to stuff pastry into a jug.
explanation.definitionFit: A flagon is a large vessel with a handle and spout for holding wine or ale.

clue.text: Where to see privileged learners melt down every so often

indicators.note: something happening every so often occurs at intervals, so only every other letter is kept

blocks.note: the second, fourth, sixth and eighth letters

explanation.surface: Privileged pupils are seen to have a tantrum now and then.
explanation.walkthrough: Melt down reads like a verb for the learners, but it is only the source of letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Eton College is an elite English boarding school whose pupils are famously privileged.

clue.text: Artwork upset tot – is it a tacky item?

indicators.note: in a down entry, upset means turned upside down, so the word reads bottom to top

blocks.note: a drawing is a piece of art
a tot is a small drink, as is a nip

explanation.surface: A child's picture has been spoiled, and someone wonders if it is tasteless.
explanation.walkthrough: Tot looks like a toddler but is a dram. Tacky here means sticky, with a sharp point that sticks into a board.
explanation.definitionFit: A thumbtack, used to fix papers to boards, is a tack in the most literal sense.

clue.text: Drained Viennese and North American sparkling wine in vessel for claret

indicators.note: drained means emptied out, so the word loses its insides and only the ends stay

blocks.note: first and last letters only
standard abbreviation
cava is Spanish sparkling wine

explanation.surface: Someone empties Viennese and American fizz into a decanter meant for claret.
explanation.walkthrough: Claret is slang for blood, so the vessel is a blood vessel, not a wine jug.
explanation.definitionFit: The vena cava is the great vein carrying blood back to the heart; claret is old slang for blood.

clue.text: Asian income picked up in Asian capital

indicators.note: picked up means heard or caught by ear, so the words are judged by their sound

blocks.note: a Thai is an Asian person, and pay is income

explanation.surface: Earnings by an Asian worker are collected in an Asian city.
explanation.definitionFit: Taipei is the capital city of Taiwan.

clue.text: Take charge of field day

blocks.note: lea is a poetic word for a meadow
standard abbreviation

explanation.surface: Someone is put in charge of a sports day.
explanation.definitionFit: To lead a group is to direct it, being the one in command.

clue.text: Abuse about a vacuous orchestrator, one unable to conduct

indicators.note: vacuous means empty, so the word is emptied of its middle and only its ends stay
about means around, so the abuse wraps round the single letter

blocks.note: to abuse someone verbally is to insult them
taken as written
first and last letters only

explanation.surface: Someone heaps abuse on a hopeless orchestrator who cannot conduct an orchestra.
explanation.walkthrough: Conduct suggests leading an orchestra, but it is conducting heat or electricity.
explanation.definitionFit: An insulator is a material that blocks the flow of electricity or heat.

clue.text: Wipe middle of vase before edges

indicators.note: the middle of a word is its central letters, with the ends left behind
to edge something is to form a border round it, so one word frames the other

blocks.note: ere is an old word for before
the two central letters

explanation.surface: Cleaning instructions: wipe the middle of a vase first, then its rim.
explanation.walkthrough: Before looks like a sequencing word, but it is the source of ERE, which edges the middle of vase.
explanation.definitionFit: To erase is to remove completely, as when wiping a board or deleting a recording.

clue.text: I perhaps love info on malfunctioning piece of AI

indicators.note: in an across entry, one thing on another comes after it, so the love and info are written second

blocks.note: HAL 9000 is the computer that goes wrong in 2001: A Space Odyssey
love is zero in tennis
gen is British slang for information

explanation.surface: Someone loves the facts about a faulty bit of artificial intelligence.
explanation.walkthrough: I looks like the first person, but it is the chemical symbol for iodine. Malfunctioning looks like an anagram signal but is part of HAL's description.
explanation.definitionFit: Iodine, symbol I, belongs to the group of elements alongside fluorine, chlorine and bromine.

clue.text: Was a vocalist on the radio covered?

indicators.note: a radio broadcast is only heard, so the words count by their sound

blocks.note: to rap is to perform rhymes over a beat

explanation.surface: A question whether a singer performed a cover version on air.
explanation.walkthrough: Covered tempts as a cover song; it is the plain sense of enclosed in paper.
explanation.definitionFit: Something wrapped is enclosed or swathed in a covering, as a parcel is.

clue.text: Intimidate country club servant

blocks.note: the United Nations is a club whose members are countries
a manservant, as in a gentleman's man

explanation.surface: Someone bullies a waiter at a country club.
explanation.walkthrough: Country club reads as a golf club; here it is an organisation of countries.
explanation.definitionFit: To unman someone is to sap their courage, making them lose nerve.

clue.text: Ring girl eating sandwiches

indicators.note: a sandwich puts its filling between two slices, so one word encloses the other

blocks.note: dining is eating a meal
gal is an informal word for a girl

explanation.surface: A boxing ring girl eats some sandwiches.
explanation.walkthrough: Ring girl reads as one phrase about boxing, but Ring stands alone as the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The expression imitates the sound a bell makes when it rings or chimes.

clue.text: Article in Bild getting complaint, going off-line?

blocks.note: der is a German definite article; Bild is a German newspaper
an ailment is an illness, a medical complaint

explanation.surface: A German tabloid piece provokes a complaint that its author is going off message.
explanation.walkthrough: Off-line suggests internet loss but means a train leaving the rails.
explanation.definitionFit: When a train comes off the rails, the accident is a derailment.

clue.text: Maybe this worker’s in grassy area, protecting a bird?

definitions.text: Maybe this worker’s in grassy area, protecting a bird?

indicators.note: protecting something means surrounding it like a shield, so one word wraps round the others

blocks.note: a garden is a lawned area
taken as written
mew is an old word for a gull

explanation.surface: A worker in the countryside guards a bird.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue describes the answer while also building it: such a worker protects wildlife in green spaces.
explanation.definitionFit: A game warden is an official who protects wild animals and birds and enforces hunting laws.

clue.text: Place for putting the shot?

blocks.note: surface reading: the athletic event of throwing a heavy metal ball
setter's reading: a shot is a picture taken with a camera, and this is where you keep such pictures

explanation.walkthrough: Putting the shot is an athletics event, so the place sounds like a stadium; shot is really a snapshot being put into a book.
explanation.definitionFit: Printed pictures are stored and displayed in a bound book with sleeves made for them.

clue.text: Cockney aspiring to fix Post Office’s counter

indicators.note: Cockney speech famously drops the h at the start of words
fixing something in place means setting it inside, so one word is lodged in the other

blocks.note: aspiring means hoping
PO is the abbreviation, with the possessive S

explanation.surface: A Londoner hopes to repair the counter at the post office.
explanation.walkthrough: Cockneys famously drop their aitches, which is why the word for aspiring loses its first letter. Counter looks like a shop counter but is an adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: Counter as an adjective means contrary or acting against, the same as opposing.

clue.text: Undressed Tony Blair partying around a noble

indicators.note: undressed means stripped of outer clothing, so the word loses its outside letters
partying suggests wild, disorderly fun, so these letters are thrown about
around means surrounding, so the jumbled letters wrap round the last word

blocks.note: the inside letters only
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A former prime minister is seen naked at a party with an aristocrat.
explanation.definitionFit: Baronial describes what belongs to or befits a baron, a member of the nobility.

clue.text: English Conservative in inept or bungling party

indicators.note: bungling means botching, so these letters are put together clumsily in a new order
in places the first pair inside the jumbled letters

blocks.note: standard abbreviation
standard abbreviation
taken as written

explanation.surface: An English Tory turns up at a party, either useless or making a mess of it.
explanation.definitionFit: A reception is a formal social gathering, such as one held after a wedding.

clue.text: Cruel around horse, but tending to rabbit

indicators.note: around means encircling, so the first word wraps round the second

blocks.note: catty means spiteful
horse is slang for heroin, abbreviated H

explanation.surface: Someone is unkind to a horse but likes rabbits.
explanation.walkthrough: To rabbit is British slang for talking on and on, from rhyming slang rabbit and pork, talk.
explanation.definitionFit: A talkative person is given to chatter, which is what rabbiting means in British slang.

clue.text: Puzzle that’s worth cracking

indicators.note: cracking something breaks it apart, so its letters fall into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A puzzle deserves solving.
explanation.walkthrough: Cracking a puzzle sounds like solving it, but here it breaks up the next word.
explanation.definitionFit: To throw someone is to disconcert or confuse them, leaving them baffled.

clue.text: Character asking for more special, unexpected events

blocks.note: Oliver Twist famously asks for more gruel in the Dickens novel
standard abbreviation

explanation.surface: A greedy character demands extra for special occasions.
explanation.definitionFit: Twists are surprising turns in a story or in events, developments no one predicted.

clue.text: He leaves the money that’s extorted in bar

indicators.note: when something leaves, it goes away, so those letters are taken out

blocks.note: taken as written
the letters removed from the following word
ransom is money demanded for releasing a captive

explanation.surface: A man walks off and leaves the extortion money in a pub.
explanation.walkthrough: THE minus HE leaves T. Bar looks like a pub but is a beam.
explanation.definitionFit: A transom is a horizontal crossbar, especially one above a door or across a window.

clue.text: Piece of rubber – it was seized by Alexander

blocks.note: first meaning: the rubber ring fitted to a wheel
second meaning: the Phoenician city Alexander the Great besieged and captured in 332 BC

explanation.walkthrough: The British spelling of the wheel covering coincides with the ancient city in modern Lebanon.
explanation.definitionFit: A tyre is a rubber casing on a wheel, and Tyre was the island city taken by Alexander after a long siege.

clue.text: One may bowl over penny-pinching reprobate

indicators.note: pinching means gripping between two points, so one word holds the other inside

blocks.note: a reprobate is a wicked person
standard abbreviation

explanation.surface: A stingy rogue might well knock someone over.
explanation.walkthrough: Bowl over looks like a phrase meaning astonish; bowl is the cricket action and over a link. A spinner is a bowler who spins the ball.
explanation.definitionFit: In cricket, a spinner is a bowler who makes the ball turn off the pitch.

clue.text: Person forced to work hasn’t left husband

indicators.note: without left, the abbreviation for it must be dropped from the word

blocks.note: a slave is compelled to labour

explanation.surface: A labourer under compulsion has stayed loyal to her husband.
explanation.walkthrough: Husband looks like a spouse, but as a verb it means to conserve. Left is L, the letter dropped.
explanation.definitionFit: To husband resources is to use them sparingly and conserve them.

clue.text: Polite refusal by king returning in shop

indicators.note: returning means going back, so the whole string reads from right to left

blocks.note: no, ta is a courteous way of declining; ta is British for thanks
R for Rex, Latin for king

explanation.surface: A monarch politely turns something down while returning goods in a store.
explanation.walkthrough: Shop looks like a store but is the slang verb for informing on someone.
explanation.definitionFit: To shop someone is British slang for betraying them to the police, which is ratting on them.

clue.text: Wannabe holy person, certainly not corrupt!

blocks.note: an emphatic refusal
to vitiate is to spoil or corrupt

explanation.surface: An aspiring saint protests that they are not corrupt at all.
explanation.definitionFit: A novitiate, or novice, is a person on probation before taking religious vows.
